name: Inositol nicotinate

lead: Inositol nicotinate is niacin bound to inositol, sold as a supplement that does not cause the usual niacin flush. Users take it as a gentler route to niacin, linking vitamin B3 to circulation and a healthier complexion.

It is described as breaking down into inositol and niacin after ingestion, and limited conversion to active niacin may explain the lack of flushing. Published research concerns circulation, including Raynaud's phenomenon and leg pain on walking, with mixed results; no study examines skin or appearance.

paras: People take it as capsules, usually daily with food, as a flush-free alternative to regular niacin, and often alongside other skin or circulation supplements. Any change in skin is judged over weeks.

Generally described as safe by mouth, with stomach upset, gas, nausea and possible liver effects similar to other niacin products. Cautions are listed for diabetes, liver or kidney disease, bleeding disorders and gout. It is sold over the counter in the US.

angle.text: Inositol nicotinate is taken as a no-flush form of niacin, with users linking vitamin B3 to better circulation and a healthier complexion. It has been studied for circulation in conditions such as intermittent claudication; nothing has been published on appearance.

lead: Inositol nicotinate, also called inositol hexanicotinate or inositol hexaniacinate, is a compound formed from niacin (vitamin B3) and inositol. In the United States it is sold as a dietary supplement, marketed as a "no-flush" form of niacin, and the body is described as breaking it down into its two components [1].

It has been studied mainly for circulation problems such as Raynaud's phenomenon and intermittent claudication rather than for skin or appearance. Wikipedia describes evidence for most other proposed uses, including cholesterol lowering, as unclear or insufficient [1]. It is listed in appearance-oriented catalogues because of its relationship to niacin, but no published study found in the sources examines its effect on skin, hair or facial appearance.

Small thermographic studies from the late 1970s and early 1980s examined its effect on digital blood flow in Raynaud's phenomenon [2][3][4], and a UK health technology assessment evaluated it alongside other drugs for intermittent claudication [5].
infobox: Sold over the counter as a supplement in the US [1]

paras: The compound has been used for peripheral circulation disorders, notably Raynaud's phenomenon and intermittent claudication, and has also been promoted for cholesterol and blood pressure. Its effectiveness for high cholesterol, high blood pressure and exercise-related leg pain is described as unclear, with mixed study results [1]. Other proposed uses, such as migraine, psoriasis and restless legs syndrome, are described as lacking sufficient supporting evidence [1].

Inositol nicotinate is reported to be metabolised to inositol and niacin after ingestion. Wikipedia notes research suggesting that the absence of flushing may relate to limited conversion to active niacin [1]. Flushing is the skin warming and redness typical of immediate-release niacin.

Taken orally it is described as generally safe, with possible stomach upset, intestinal gas and nausea, and liver damage similar to other niacin products [1]. Cautions listed include diabetes (possible rise in blood sugar), liver or kidney disease, bleeding disorders or upcoming surgery, and gout [1].

Several small studies in Raynaud's phenomenon used thermography to assess digital blood flow and temperature during inositol nicotinate treatment, published in the Journal of International Medical Research in 1977, 1979 and 1981 [2][3][4]. A review of Raynaud's pharmacotherapy and a BMJ Clinical Evidence summary of secondary Raynaud's discuss the drug class and treatment options [6][7]. A health technology assessment published in 2011 evaluated cilostazol, naftidrofuryl oxalate, pentoxifylline and inositol nicotinate for intermittent claudication in peripheral arterial disease [5].
No studies found that examine inositol nicotinate for skin, hair or facial appearance.
